close_reason: Replaced i64::try_from(unix).expect() with .unwrap_or(i64::MAX) in unix_to_rfc3339. Overflowing u64 inputs saturate to i64::MAX (year ~292 billion) and emit a well-formed multi-digit-year RFC 3339 date with deterministic output. The civil_from_days arithmetic is i64 throughout and stays in range. Documented as 'never panics' on any u64 input. Regression test covers three boundary inputs (i64::MAX, i64::MAX+1, u64::MAX) and asserts no-panic + ASCII output + saturation determinism. 296 tests pass; clippy clean.
description:
pkix-lint/src/oscal/emit.rs:851-855: i64::try_from(unix).expect('unix seconds out of i64 range') panics for any unix > i64::MAX. The rustdoc dismisses this as 'in practice the cap is u64::MAX and no realistic input triggers it' — true for wall-clock time today, false for attacker-controlled JSON input.

Trigger: EvaluationReport carries evaluated_at_unix: u64 directly from caller input. A malicious or malformed JSON Finding payload (or an OSCAL Profile composition that sets evaluated_at_unix to a value above 9.2 × 10^18) will panic the emitter mid-OSCAL-write, killing any host process emitting evidence packs from untrusted inputs.

Maintainer consequence: same shape as the cert_sha256_hex panic (PKIX-7f92.1) — a host process that handles untrusted Findings or EvaluationReports can be DOSed via JSON. The deserializer trusts u64 (correct range) but the formatter then panics on the high half.

Fix: change the formatter to take u64 internally and saturate or return a sentinel ('+overflow') for values that don't fit, rather than panicking. The civil_from_days algorithm itself wants i64 arithmetic, but the input clamp lives in a single function and is easy to swap to .unwrap_or(i64::MAX) with a sentinel year suffix.
title: unix_to_rfc3339 panics on u64 timestamps above i64::MAX
